'''Valerian Illarionovich Tatarskii''' (Russian: Валериа́н Илларио́нович Тата́рский) was a Soviet and American physicist who worked on the theory of [[wave propagation]] in random media (WPRM). His theoretical work provided the statistical framework for understanding how turbulence in the atmosphere and ocean affects light, radio, and acoustic waves, used in fields such as [[adaptive optics]], [[remote sensing]], and free-space [[optical communications]].<ref name="Obituary"/>

==Early life and career==
Tatarskii was born on 6 February 1929 in [[Moscow]]. Following his graduation from [[Lomonosov Moscow State University]] in 1952,<ref name="OSA"/> he joined the [[Institute of Atmospheric Physics]] (IAP) of the [[USSR Academy of Sciences]] in Moscow. His early research on [[turbulence modeling]] was influenced by the work of Soviet scientists like [[Andrey Kolmogorov]] and [[Alexander Obukhov]] (who served as Tatarskii's doctoral advisor).<ref name="Obituary"/><ref name="MGP-Courant"/>

He completed his [[Candidate of Sciences]] (a Ph.D. equivalent) thesis in 1957 and his [[Doctor of Sciences]] (a "higher doctorate") thesis in 1965. Both focused on the statistical theory of wave propagation in turbulent media.<ref name="Chase"/>

==Scientific contributions==
Tatarskii's contribution was the creation of a comprehensive, rigorous statistical theory explaining the effects of random, small-scale fluctuations (turbulence) in the atmosphere on propagating waves.

===Monographs===
* ''Wave Propagation in a Turbulent Medium''. New York: McGraw-Hill. (Original Russian edition published 1959; English edition 1961).
* ''The Effects of the Turbulent Atmosphere on Wave Propagation''. Jerusalem: Israel Program for Scientific Translations. (Original Russian edition published 1967; English edition 1971).

These books developed the mathematical tools required to characterize wave [[distortion]], including [[phase shift]] and intensity fluctuations ([[twinkling|scintillation]]).

===Theoretical methods===
Tatarskii worked on several theoretical methods for solving WPRM problems:
* Method of Smooth Perturbations ([[Rytov approximation]]).<ref name="Farrell"/><ref name="Tatarskii1961"/>
* He adapted the formal mathematical apparatus of [[Feynman diagram]]s from quantum field theory to solve the higher-order [[method of moments (electromagnetics)|moment equations]] for wave fields in strongly random media.<ref name="Farrell"/>
* He introduced a Markov approximation to simplify the description of [[wave scattering]], enabling the treatment of strong intensity fluctuations.<ref name="Farrell"/>
* Tatarskii applied [[Richard Feynman]]'s [[path integral formulation]] to the [[parabolic partial differential equation|parabolic wave equation]], offering an alternative approach to problems of strong turbulence.<ref name="Farrell"/>

==Later career and recognition==
In 1990, Tatarskii emigrated to the United States, where he joined the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] (NOAA) Environmental Technology Laboratory (ETL) in Boulder, Colorado. His work there focused on the application of statistical wave theory to [[remote sensing]] and [[atmospheric sounding]].<ref name="Obituary"/>

He was a founding member and associate editor of the international journal ''[[Waves in Random Media]]''.<ref name="Obituary"/>

===Honors and awards===
* 1976: Corresponding Member of the [[USSR Academy of Sciences]]<ref name="PhysicsToday"/>
* 1990: [[USSR State Prize]]<ref name="PhysicsToday"/>
* 1991: [[Fellow of the Optical Society of America]] (OSA)<ref name="PhysicsToday"/>
* 1994: [[Max Born Award]] from the OSA, cited for "pioneering and fundamental theoretical contributions to the statistical theory of wave propagation in the atmosphere."<ref name="OSA"/>
* 1994: Foreign Associate of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (NAE) of the USA<ref name="NAE_Page"/>

==Selected publications==
* Tatarskii, V. I., & Zavorotny, V. U. (1980). Strong Fluctuations in the Intensity of Waves Propagating in Random Media. ''Progress in Optics'', 18, 204–256.
* Tatarskii, V. I., & Galkin, I. G. (1997). The Application of Path Integrals to Wave Propagation in Random Media. ''Waves in Random Media'', 7(1), 1–25.

==Death==
Valerian Tatarskii died on 3 October 2020, at the age of 91.<ref name="Obituary"/>
